Why should Ethereum reduce its issuance?

In essence, stake participation is growing beyond requirements for economic security, and paying people to do something that is not necessary always comes with downsides:

1. By maintaining the current reward curve, Ethereum compels participants to incur higher costs than necessary for securing the network (costs broadly defined to include hardware, assumed risks, reduced liquidity, taxes, etc.). Reducing issuance will improve welfare by eliminating implied costs that may very well amount to more than a billion dollars per year.

2. If everyone stakes, some LSTs may become “too big to fail”, and the social layer may be incapable of upholding the intended consensus process. Proliferation of LSTs can also impede ETH as trustless money, making Ethereum less appealing to rely and build on due to the risk of future monopolistic pressure.

Let’s take a closer look at these two points.

full_text:
1: Reduced costs raise welfare

The figure shows a hypothetical future supply curve in blue, indicating the amount of stake deposited D at various staking yields y. It captures the implied marginal cost of staking. Every ETH holder is positioned along the supply curve according to how high a cost they assign to staking, with their required yield reflecting that cost. Relevant costs include hardware and other resources, upkeep, the acquisition and deployment of technical knowledge, illiquidity, trust in third parties and other factors increasing the risk premium, various opportunity costs, taxes, etc. The area below the supply curve therefore represents these costs.

By reducing issuance and going from the black curve to the green curve, the dark blue cost area (around 450 000 ETH) is removed, thus improving welfare. The issued ETH covered for hardware expenses, taxes, reduced liquidity, and risks that users would choose to sidestep under a lower yield. With the green curve, they can, and the benefits are shared by everyone, including remaining stakers.

There is also a surplus shift from stakers to everyone from a change in issuance policy, indicated by the darker grey area. That ETH previously benefited stakers, since it was taken from everyone (in the form of newly minted ETH), and then given specifically to them. It is common to treat the issuance reduction achieved by removing the dark blue area the same as when removing the dark grey area. In this case, value may appear to merely shift from one class of users to another, and the welfare gain can get lost in translation. But removing that blue area hurts no one and benefits everyone, thus leading to improved welfare.

What happens when we impose unnecessary costs on our users? If they are forced to choose between incurring these costs as stakers or subjecting themselves to increased dilution under equilibrium, they might simply decide to use another blockchain, where the imposed costs are lower. This would of course affect both token holders and anyone building on Ethereum negatively. Ethereum operates in a free market and must always strive to perfect the user experience.

full_text:
2: Macro perspective

An LST exceeding critical thresholds regarding the proportion of stake under its control may compromise the consensus mechanism and derive outsized profits. But if everyone is compelled to stake, an entity or cartel of entities may also gain control over a significant proportion of the total ETH---propelled by network externalities such as the money function of an LST. The leverage point sits outside of the consensus mechanism, as does the compromised institution, namely the social layer.

It became apparent with The DAO that if the proportion of the total circulating supply affected by an outcome grows sufficiently large, then the social layer may waver on its commitment to the intended consensus process. An LST might grow too big to fail in the eyes of the Ethereum social layer. Warning systems and recourses based on a functioning social layer could lose their effectiveness. Staking becomes so ubiquitous that the social consensus mechanism itself is overloaded.

If one or a few LSTs overtake as money in the Ethereum ecosystem, they will embed themselves across every layer and application. An economy that is not powered by a trustless asset is arguably not as resilient, regardless of whether the consensus process itself is never threatened. The applications powering the money will gain an outsized influence over the applications using the money, and Ethereum will become a less desirable blockchain to build and rely on.

full_text:
1) How do you see the trade-off between the social, political, and neutrality costs of issuance changes vs the potential benefit of any particular change?

2) What if the percentage of staked ETH never exceeds ~40% for the next five years? Would this change your view on impetus for an issuance change?

3) The LST competitive landscape is maturing and Lido's market share is down to 29%. If this trajectory continued and Lido share was down to ~22% within three years, does this change your view on the risk of LST monopoly as motivation for an issuance change?

4) In your view, does the stakesure paper from Sreeram et al hold any potential to completely remove inflationary block rewards? What would staked ETH yield and staking participation look like if stakesure works and was adopted? Could stakesure become the preferred "issuance change"?

Thanks again for these very thoughtful questions and sorry for my late reply.

1. Yes, there is indeed a “switching cost” when changing issuance. This cost does not only come at the social or political level. Compromising economic agents’ ability to plan ahead is welfare-degrading in general.
When it comes to neutrality, I think that the current issuance policy is only “neutral” in the sense that it was the initial design. It is arguably not neutral in its ability to allocate an appropriate amount of newly minted tokens to ensure security. There is no reasonable limit on the deposit ratio, which can over time become much higher than what is necessary for security. Indeed, since issuance scales by the square root of staking deposits, the cost to Ethereum in the form of issuance will continue to rise even when deposits have gone beyond security requirements. Moreover, they will continue to rise even when additional staking could make the protocol less secure (as discussed in terms of short-term security in the FAQ).

This does not seem like a policy that offers a neutral balance between stakers and non-stakers. It would seem more reasonable for issuance to fall when deposits exceed security requirements, or at least remain stable. I think that this aspect of “neutrality” might gain more attention if Ethereum remains inflationary going forward. Even if the inflation rate alone is not critical for determining if Ethereum takes on too high costs to secure the network, it can still shift the sociopolitical landscape. It might highlight how high issuance forces users to incur additional costs as stakers, or otherwise see their holdings eroded over time (as discussed in the FAQ).

When faced with these trade-offs, it is not clear that I, as a researcher, should approach the topic like a “politician”, i.e., only pursuing or advocating for the policies that are most popular in the short term (at least among the most vocal participants). History is full of examples where an expansive monetary policy was politically expedient in the short run, but turned out to be detrimental to society in the long run. As I have said before, excessive incentives for staking, beyond what is necessary for security, can unfortunately over time turn into perverse subsidies. Issuance policy will influence what kind of applications that get built on Ethereum, and the neutral position then is arguably to only issue tokens when necessary for ensuring security (but security does indeed involve keeping Ethereum staking decentralized and solo staking viable, that is not to be forgotten).

Therefore, I will as a researcher continue to advocate for the policies I see as best for Ethereum, which involve tempering issuance. The social and political trade-offs will then become evident in dialogue with the community. My concern in this regard is that while a reduction in issuance can benefit the many, “vested financial interests” will predominantly drive the debate.

2. I have long held the position that we are heading towards 40-50 million ETH staked within this time frame, so this would not necessarily change my view on the issue that much. I held the same position during the EIP-7514 discussion as well. If we were at around 40% in five years without having changed issuance policy, I would consider this an unfortunate result of indecision, because we could have tempered issuance and been at around 25-30% (with lower costs). Of course, seeing this level of stake in five years means that the worst-case scenarios have not come to fruition which is good. So it does mean something and would still affect my view. But it also means that the best-case scenario of not growing much at all did not materialize. If never exceeding 40% means staying between 25-30%, then it would indeed change my view.

3. Yes then the rationale of stemming LST monopolies would be a bit weakened. Still, it would not mean that such a monopoly cannot emerge on even longer time frames, say as costs of staking decrease further, and the deposit ratio rises. That said, the primary argument for an issuance reduction is cost reduction. And to be clear, the argument is not about Lido specifically. If another LST were to dominate instead, it could be even more problematic depending on its characteristics. Furthermore, the issue of monopolies is not just about LSTs. Restaking presents another potential risk (for example, I do not agree with Eigenlayer’s position, which seems to be that there is no risk associated with all stake being locked up with them).

4. I would have to get back to this question later. I do not think it can become the preferred issuance change.

full_text:
Thanks for your responses!

I'm generally in favor of an issuance change that satisfies all of these criteria, and I think others would be, too:
- We are extremely certain it will be the last issuance change ever needed. A permanent solution.
- We've successfully built broad social consensus around the change, it's not controversial, except perhaps with groups like Lido where they directly lose money from the change.
- We moved at an appropriately glacial pace to have many independent researchers analyze the solution and drive confidence it will be a healthy permanent solution, and give lots of time for the community to socialize and prepare for the issuance change. I see 1559 as a success story here where the spec was nailed down year(s) (??) before mainnet activation and that gave a lot of time for healthy discourse and formation of common knowledge. The Roughgarden paper was particularly excellent as a coordination point.
- Obviously, the issuance change must be expected to meaningfully reduce issuance.

Given these criteria, I strongly agree that doing the change sooner than later is much better for the long-term political and institutional stability of ethereum. So I see the tension between doing this as soon as possible vs. the criterion to move at a glacial pace.

Perhaps a useful rule of thumb here may be that the spec for the issuance change can be nailed down at least one hard fork before it ends up being deployed.

Personally, I think Pectra will launch in perhaps Q2/3 2025. Maybe we could finalize the spec for an issuance change by Q2 2025, and then seek to include it in the next hard fork after Pectra or even the one after that.
